generation.hypothesis: For a high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating on a transition metal matrix, tribological performance (wear resistance) will initially increase with rising ambient temperature up to a critical threshold, after which it will degrade rapidly. The dominant mechanism linking thermal conditions to wear resistance is the thermally activated formation of a protective, self-healing oxide layer (tribo-oxide) on the coating surface. At low to moderate elevated temperatures (e.g., 200°C to 600°C), the diffusion of alloying elements (such as Al, Cr, Ti) is sufficient to form a continuous, adherent oxide scale that reduces the coefficient of friction and prevents direct asperity contact, thereby increasing wear resistance. As temperature increases further, the mechanism shifts: the oxide layer may become too thick and brittle, leading to spallation, or the underlying matrix may undergo softening (loss of solid solution strengthening) or phase instability, causing the protective layer to fail. The boundary where performance degrades is predicted to occur when the rate of oxide spallation exceeds the rate of oxide formation, or when the matrix yield strength drops below the critical stress required to support the contact load, typically occurring above 600–700°C for many Al/Cr-containing HEAs, or potentially lower for refractory HEAs if oxidation resistance is poor.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi-based or refractory-based) deposited on a transition metal matrix substrate (e.g., steel or Ti-alloy), with a microstructure potentially containing solid solution phases and/or precipitates (FCC/BCC/L12 depending on composition).
generation.intervention: Subject the coated system to reciprocating or sliding wear tests at incrementally increasing ambient temperatures (e.g., 25°C, 200°C, 400°C, 600°C, 800°C) under controlled atmospheric conditions (air).
generation.conditions: Atmospheric pressure, air environment, sliding speed 0.1–1.0 m/s, normal load 5–20 N, temperature range 25°C to 800°C.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface oxide layer (tribo-oxide) composition and morphology, and the underlying coating microstructure (grain size, precipitate stability).
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles and supported by PMC7515071: Wear resistance is governed by the competition between the formation of a protective oxide layer (which reduces friction and wear) and the mechanical stability of the coating. At elevated temperatures, diffusion rates increase, promoting the formation of a continuous oxide scale (e.g., Al2O3, Cr2O3). This layer acts as a solid lubricant and barrier. However, beyond a critical temperature, thermal expansion mismatch and oxide brittleness lead to spallation, exposing the softer underlying metal to abrasive wear. Additionally, thermal softening of the HEA matrix reduces its load-bearing capacity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Wear rate will decrease by 30–50% as temperature rises from 25°C to ~500°C due to oxide layer formation. The coefficient of friction (COF) will decrease slightly. Above ~600°C, wear rate will increase sharply (by >200% relative to peak performance) due to oxide spallation and matrix softening. The transition boundary is estimated at 600–700°C for Al/Cr-rich HEAs.
generation.baseline: Wear rate at 25°C (ambient) for the same coating system.
generation.boundary: Critical temperature T_crit ≈ 600–700°C, where the protective oxide layer fails to maintain integrity or the matrix yield strength drops below the contact stress.
generation.uncertainty: The exact boundary temperature depends heavily on the specific HEA composition (e.g., Al content for Al2O3 formation, Cr for Cr2O3) and the coating microstructure (grain size, porosity). Refractory HEAs (Nb/Mo/W based) may have a higher T_crit but suffer from poor oxidation resistance at lower temperatures, shifting the boundary down. The substrate thermal conductivity may also influence the local interface temperature.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct wear tests on the HEA coating at 25°C, 500°C, and 750°C. Simultaneously, perform in-situ or post-test surface analysis (XRD, SEM/EDS) to quantify the oxide layer thickness, composition, and adherence. Additionally, measure the hardness of the coating at these temperatures to correlate with wear rates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the wear rate does not show a minimum in the 400–600°C range (i.e., if wear rate monotonically increases or decreases with temperature) OR if the oxide layer remains adherent and protective at 750°C without a corresponding increase in wear rate, OR if the wear rate increases at 500°C despite the presence of a continuous oxide layer (indicating a different dominant mechanism like severe plastic deformation or phase transformation).

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
